items.quote: the Paracelsian Theory of Chymicall Physick as yet is wrapt up in perplexities and some obscurities which are not easie to all
items.note: The text says the Paracelsian theory is still wrapped in obscurities not easy to all readers.

items.quote: learn of Paracelsus and other Chymists to prepare and make up their Medicines, but to observe the method of Hippocrates in curing diseases
items.note: Croll advises students of Physick to take preparation of medicines from the Chymists and the method of curing from Hippocrates.

items.name: Paracelsus
items.quote: learn of Paracelsus and other Chymists
items.note: Paracelsus named as the teacher of medicine preparation.

items.name: Hippocrates
items.quote: observe the method of Hippocrates in curing diseases
items.note: Hippocrates named as the source of the method of curing.

items.quote: these two Schools of Old and New Physick may be reconcil'd without contradiction
items.what: two Schools of Old and New Physick
items.note: The text sets apart two schools of Physick and holds they can be joined in one physician.

items.quote: they would not be so shy to black their hands
items.note: Croll wants physicians to do the hand-work of preparing medicines themselves.

items.quote: avoyd idlenes because it is the Devils cushon, the mother of vice & the step-mother of virtue
items.note: Margin note condemns idleness.

items.quote: By the contempt of sciences we lose the good and get the evill.
items.note: Margin note: despising the sciences brings loss of the good.

items.quote: if he administer any thing it is to be accounted of as the hand of God; but if he be a wretched Miscreant, and an Ignoramus, what he giveth is to be lookt upon as poyson
items.note: The same giving of medicine is God's hand or poison depending on the physician.

items.quote: cannot indure that Physick with its preparations should premiscuously be imparted to all sorts of men, for fear if it should be made common, or as they say Prophaned, they should lose their gaines
items.note: Many physicians want Physick and its preparations withheld from common people for gain; Croll reports this to reject it.

items.quote: tis a foolish conceit of the frantick vulgar sort, who think that a Secret looseth its vertue when tis made known
items.note: Croll rejects the belief that a secret loses its virtue by being made known.

items.quote: neither God nor Nature hath made every man a Physitian
items.note: Croll answers the fear of disclosure: not everyone is fitted to be a physician.

items.quote: rightly administer some known Physick to the Patient according to art and the methodicall and set proportion or quantity of the Dose
items.note: Administering a known medicine by art and by the set quantity of the dose.

items.quote: imitate that most commendable and religious custome of the Hermetick Physitians, who always use to pray for a blessing upon their endeavours
items.note: Physicians should follow the Hermetick Physitians in praying for a blessing on their work.

items.quote: Whosoever useth any Creature without craving a blissing, God imputeth it to him for no other than theft and rapine.
items.note: Using any creature without asking a blessing counts before God as theft.

items.name: the Doctor of the Gentiles
items.quote: so the Doctor of the Gentiles commandeth the Colossians, saying; Whatsoever yee do in word or deed,
items.note: Words given to the Doctor of the Gentiles to the Colossians, supporting administering in the name of Jesus.

items.name: Col.
items.note: Margin note names the writings beside the quoted command.

items.name: our Creator
items.quote: Call upon me in the day of thy trouble, I will deliver thee, and thou shalt glorifie me, saith our Creator.
items.note: Words given to the Creator, supporting that God's blessing is obtained by prayer.

items.quote: The best and chiefest Foundation of Physick is faith in God, and love to our neighbour, if this be wanting all Art is nothing worth.
items.note: Margin note: faith and love are the foundation of Physick; without them art is worthless.

items.quote: Paracelsus would not have Physick be concealed.
items.note: Margin note: Paracelsus opposed concealing Physick.

items.name: Paracelsus
items.quote: Paracelsus would not have Physick be concealed.
items.note: Margin note gives Paracelsus a view against concealment.

items.quote: Paracelsus would not have Physick be concealed.
items.note: Paracelsus is said to want Physick unconcealed, while CH5.61 says the Paracelsian theory is still wrapped in obscurities not easy to all.

items.quote: though all experiences are secrets, yet Novices know not the Dose and true quantity in which the vertue of Physick consisteth
items.note: Margin note: experiences are secrets, and novices lack knowledge of the dose, where the virtue lies.

items.quote: if we take too much Saffron or Treacle it is poyson, if too little it will doe no good
items.note: Margin note: the quantity taken decides whether a medicine harms, helps or does nothing.

items.quote: before we give or take any Physick we are to pray to the good and great God
items.note: First point: prayer before giving or taking medicine.

items.quote: after we have recovered and made them well, let us never cease to give him hearty thanks
items.note: Second point: thanksgiving after recovery.

items.quote: These two poynts are scarce thought of by most Physitians, which is the chief cause of thier ill successe
items.note: Prayer and thanksgiving are numbered as two points and made the chief cause of physicians' failure when neglected.

items.quote: though a Cathartick medicine doth work equally effectually in a knave as it doth in an honest man
items.note: A medicine's working is the same in good and bad men.

items.quote: For what medicine soever it be that is administred and taken without imploring the Divine Grace
items.note: Medicine taken without asking divine grace turns to a worse disease for the impenitent.

items.name: Ecel.
items.note: Margin note names a writing beside the passage.

items.quote: sometimes the sick person is not recovered by the best and fittest medicines that can be applyed, and that for these eight causes
items.note: The text announces a numbered list of eight causes why the best medicines fail.

items.quote: First, Because the Terme of Life approacheth, which cannot be prolong'd by any art or help of Man.
items.note: First cause: the end of life set for a person.

items.quote: there is one thing that hindereth corruption, reneweth youth, and prolongeth the short life, as in the Patriarchs
items.note: An unnamed one thing is said to hinder corruption and prolong life; the lines given do not name it.

items.quote: No Medicine can preserve the corruptible body from death
items.note: No medicine preserves the body from death, yet one thing is said to hinder corruption and renew youth; the text then limits it by the decree that all must die.

items.quote: as we shall shew anon, the life may be shortned or lengthned
items.note: Points forward to a later place on shortening and lengthening life.

items.name: Plato
items.quote: least with Plato we conclude a recesse after such a time
items.note: A view given to Plato, set aside by Croll.

items.quote: in this case the universall and chiefest medicine is of no effect
items.note: A single chief medicine is named and said to fail against the set end of life.

items.quote: can perpetuate the wedlock of life and death, which by an immutable necessity is destin'd to a divorce
items.note: Life in the body spoken of as a marriage bound to end in divorce.

items.name: Paracels.
items.quote: Paracels. lib. de resuscitatione naturalium, sol. 295.
items.note: Margin note names a writing of Paracelsus beside the first cause.

items.quote: Our domestick enemy which we beat about usis the cause of our death.
items.note: Margin note names an unnamed inner enemy as the cause of death.

items.quote: The Curse in the Creature is removed by death.
items.note: Margin note: death removes the curse in the creature.

items.quote: Secondly, Because through the ignorance of unskilfull Physitians, and their naughty medicines, the sick is brought to that passe, that the disease is corrupt, pernicious, and incurable
items.note: Second cause: bad physicians have made the disease incurable.

items.quote: And to such commonly the Chymists are sent for
items.note: Chymists are called only when the case is already lost.

items.name: Plutarch
items.quote: whom Plutarch calls Physitians of Trophilus, who said that he was a compleat Physitian who could judg what might be done, and what not
items.note: Plutarch and Trophilus cited: a complete physician knows what can and cannot be done.

items.quote: Let them take heed also they mix not their own medicines with others poyson, least the miscarriage be ascribed to the good and the recovery to the bad
items.note: Chymists should not mix their medicines with others' to avoid false blame and credit.

items.name: these men
items.quote: such as these men commonly (and justly) call Honest Hangmen
items.note: A common name for physicians who let a patient die rather than allow another credit.

items.quote: Thirdly, Because the Physitian is sent for too late, when Nature is overcome and the disease hath got the mastery
items.note: Third cause: the physician is called too late.

items.quote: the expected fruit of health would have sprung up
items.note: Medicine cast in early is spoken of as sowing that yields health as fruit.

items.quote: Fourthly, Because the sick doth not follow directions
items.note: Fourth cause: the patient's disorderly living.

items.name: Aelianus
items.quote: the Golden law of the Locrians recorded by Aelianus
items.note: A law of the Locrians cited from Aelianus against disorderly living.

items.quote: Fifthly, Because some mens Natures or peculiar qualityes are not so easy to be cured
items.note: Fifth cause: hard natures and a contrary season.

items.quote: the Time or Season, together with the bad inclination of the Astra's is very crosse and contrary to the health
items.note: The season and the Astra's can work against health.

items.quote: For whatsoever is cured before the time is subject to a relaps tis a very instant of the Season or time of the harvest only that makes a sure and certaine cure
items.note: A sure cure depends on the right moment; early cures relapse.

items.quote: A ripe pear or apple will fall of its own accord, but before wee shake the tree in vaine to get it down.
items.note: Ripe fruit as an image for the right time of cure.

items.quote: especially in the cure of Astrall diseases
items.note: A kind of disease named as Astrall, where timing counts most.

items.quote: make it their chiefe care that they doe no hurt when they can doe no good
items.note: Physicians should at least do no harm.

items.quote: in summer one course is to be taken, in winter another, in Autumn another
items.note: Margin note: the cure changes with the season.

items.quote: Sixthly, Because diseases are come to their appoynted period, and then by the Lawes of Nature there can be no recovery
items.note: Sixth cause: the disease has reached its set end.

items.quote: perfect, absolute and compleat bituminous, Colar, stony and sandy coagulations
items.note: Completed coagulations named as incurable diseases.

items.quote: what Nature hath once taken away the Physitian can by no means restore
items.note: The physician cannot restore what Nature has taken away.

items.quote: None can reform the errours of Nature.
items.note: Margin note restating the sixth cause.

items.quote: Seventhly, As the base nigardlynesse of the sick (though there is no money more honestly got, and more unwillingly parted with) make the Physitian negligent in his office
items.note: Seventh cause opens with the patient's stinginess.

items.quote: the sick parties doubt, distrust, and unbeliefe of the Physitians diligence and care, doth either retard the effect of the Physick
items.note: The patient's distrust slows or blocks the medicine.

items.quote: think to be made well by God (though indeed he be the onely Physitian) without the use of Means by which he worketh
items.note: Croll rejects refusing medicine in favour of God alone; God works by means.

items.quote: There is a twofold Physick; Visible or created, and Invisible even the WORD of GOD
items.note: The text divides Physick into visible created medicine and the invisible Word of God.

items.quote: he that saith Physick is worth nothing, doth upon the matter affirm that there is no God
items.note: Denying medicine is made equal to denying God.

items.quote: Physitians should take nothing of the poor for their Physick
items.note: Margin note: no fee from the poor.

items.name: Ecclesiastic
items.quote: Ecclesiastic: 38.
items.note: Margin note names a writing beside the ordinance of God.

items.quote: The Physitian and the Physick are the very true mercy of God.
items.note: Margin note: physician and medicine are God's mercy.

items.quote: Moreover, as hath been said, the Mind of the Patient being raised with much confidence doth take the Physick with a stronger desire
items.note: Points back to an earlier place on the patient's confidence.

items.name: Hippocrates
items.quote: it was not without cause that Hippocrates in his Aphorismes speaketh so much of the Confidence of the sick in the Physitian and his Physick.
items.note: Hippocrates cited for the patient's confidence.

items.quote: A firm Faith, undoubted Hope, Love and Confidence toward the Physitian and his Physick, doth very much conduce to health, yea sometimes more than the Physitian and his Physick too.
items.note: The patient's faith can do more than the physician and medicine.

items.quote: Naturall Faith (I speak not of the Faith of Grace by Christ) inborn of God the Father in the first Creation, which is our IMAGINATION
items.note: The text says Naturall Faith, distinct from faith of grace, is our Imagination.

items.quote: is so powerfull that it can both cause and cure diseases, as is plaine in time of Pestilence
items.note: Imagination both causes and cures disease, shown in plague.

items.quote: it breedeth that Basilisk of Heaven, which intoxicateth the microcosmicall Firmament from his own superstition
items.note: Fear-bred imagination named a Basilisk of Heaven poisoning the inner firmament.

items.quote: The Naturall Plague becomes Firmamental and supernaturall, that is to say, when the Iliaster or Evestrum of the Sun, provoked by the sins of men to wrath and punishment
items.note: The text explains when plague becomes firmamental: the Iliaster or Evestrum of the Sun, provoked by sin.

items.quote: because of the singular participarion it hath with the Evester of Man
items.note: The Evestrum of the Sun shares in an Evester of Man.

items.quote: it infecteth the Mummy and Sulphur of the microcosm, Man, who hiddenly possesseth all innate macrocosmicall poysons
items.note: Plague infects the Mummy and Sulphur of man, who holds within all the poisons of the great world.

items.quote: That Physitian doth most good of whom most
items.note: Margin note: the physician most trusted does most good (rest partly illegible).

items.name: Eccl.
items.note: Margin note names a writing beside sorrow as venom of life.

items.quote: The Stars are the rods of the Astra's.
items.note: Margin note distinguishes Stars from Astra's: the stars are their rods.

items.name: Paracels.
items.quote: Paracels. tract. 2.
items.note: Margin note names a writing of Paracelsus beside the plague passage.

items.quote: Such is the force of the Sydereall spirit upon the body, that whithersoever it imagineth and dreameth it carryeth and leadeth the very body up and down with it, as we see in Noctambulaters.
items.note: The Sydereall spirit moves the body where it imagines, as in sleepwalkers.

items.quote: but how that comes to passe cannot be searched out
items.note: How faith works by God is said to be beyond searching.

items.quote: Faith is at least a work, I mean his work in whom we believe.
items.note: The text says in what sense faith is a work.

items.quote: The Cogitations surpasse and goe beyond the Operations of the Astra's and Elements
items.note: Thoughts exceed the workings of the Astra's and elements.

items.quote: the Imagination giveth a Sydus or Constellation, the Sydus, (by reason of the Matrimony with the Imagination) giveth the effect or work.
items.note: A chain: faith gives imagination, imagination a Sydus, the Sydus the effect.

items.quote: The Will and Imagination of Man is the mother of the plague
items.note: Margin note: will and imagination breed plague.

items.quote: Read Paracel of invisible diseases, and the efficacy of the faith of Nature, which by God can do all things Naturally.
items.note: Margin note sends the reader to a writing of Paracelsus on invisible diseases.

items.quote: To mix Faith with the Physick is that which giveth spirit to the Physick, the spirit gives the knowledge of the Physick, the Physick gives health.
items.what: To mix Faith with the Physick
items.note: A chain from faith through spirit and knowledge to health.

items.quote: I mean the Spirit of Nature or the Sydus of the medicine
items.note: The text says which Spirit it means: the Spirit of Nature, the Sydus of the medicine.

items.quote: as we saw some years since in that famous Anwalding Panacaea
items.note: A named panacea whose cures are put down to faith.

items.quote: that new medicinall Spring which brake out this yeare in the coasts of Misnia and Bohemia
items.note: A healing spring of that year, its cures put down to faith.

items.quote: For the rational soul rouzed up and inflamed with a vehement imagination overcometh even Nature it selfe
items.note: Vehement imagination of the soul overcomes nature, in one's own body and others'.

items.quote: For by her Imagination she formeth the infant, as a Potter doth the clay.
items.note: A pregnant woman's imagination shapes the child.

items.quote: the Astra's of the microcosmicall Firmament, or the Astra's of the humane Mind
items.note: The inner Astra's are equated with the Astra's of the human mind.

items.quote: The Imagination is like pitch, it easily sticketh
items.note: Margin note: imagination clings like pitch.

items.quote: many through overmuch joy or too much sorrow, by too much love or hatred, have dyed, and many times by the like passions have been cured of long diseases
items.note: Strong passions can kill or cure.

items.name: Avicen
items.quote: as Avicen saith, Nature obeyeth the cogitations and vehement desires of the Soul
items.note: Avicen cited: nature obeys the soul's thoughts and desires.

items.quote: good words are the Physitians of a sick Soul
items.note: Margin note: words heal the soul.

items.quote: Unbeliefe is the greatest and most powerfull enemy of Faith: For the Imagination joyned with Faith can do all things.
items.note: Margin note: imagination with faith can do all things; unbelief opposes it.

items.name: the woman that had the bloody issue
items.quote: the aforesaid Naturall Faith its efficacy manifested it selfe in the woman that had the bloody issue, and in the Centurion
items.note: Examples from Holy Writ for Naturall Faith; also points back to it as aforesaid.

items.quote: It is well known to all what great matters a constant Credulity in an elevated or raised Mind can doe by a strong imagination
items.note: Steady belief with strong imagination does great things.

items.quote: as well in Superstition as in true Religion, and enervate the desired effect even of the most powerfull Experiments
items.note: Doubt weakens every work, whether superstitious or religious, even strong experiments.

items.name: Holy Writ
items.quote: our Saviour, as Holy Writ saith, was not able to work miracles in Capernaum, because they believed not
items.note: Holy Writ cited: unbelief stopped miracles.

items.quote: so likewise God will doe nothing without Man, as his Organ or Instument, God and the Creature both together, neither without the other.
items.note: God works through man as instrument.

items.name: Mar.
items.quote: Mar. 13.58. Marke 6.5.
items.note: Margin note names writings beside the Capernaum passage.

items.quote: Eightly, Least the sick party recovering should commit greater sins against God, his neighbor and himselfe to the losse of his Soul
items.note: Eighth cause: recovery might lead to greater sin.

items.quote: every sicknesse is as it were an expiation or propitiatory of sacrifice
items.note: Sickness is said to be a kind of expiation.

items.quote: sins weaken the powers of the Soul, and make it impotent to the Naturall Government of the body
items.note: Sin weakens the soul's rule over the body and hastens death.

items.quote: Or else the sick is held under this yoke and bridle of infirmity, as by a wholsome Purgatory
items.note: Illness called a wholesome Purgatory.

items.name: Job
items.note: Margin note names a writing beside the eighth cause.

items.quote: no Corporall medicine (because God hath shut the doors of Nature) can do any good, but onely Celestiall and spirituall
items.note: Diseases from God's wrath yield only to spiritual remedy.

items.quote: by serious repentance, heartily to bewaile the sins that we have committed, to allay the provoked wrath of God by Amendment of life and Reconciliation to our neighbor
items.note: The spiritual cure: repentance, amendment, reconciliation.

items.name: Paracelsus
items.quote: Paracelsus calleth them Deal diseases, which are from the Ens of God
items.note: Paracelsus' name for diseases sent by God.

items.quote: Paracelsus calleth them Deal diseases, which are from the Ens of God, who inflicteth all such diseases
items.note: Deal diseases are defined as those from the Ens of God.

items.name: Paracelsus
items.quote: the Cure, saith he, is by Faith, or when the purging is perfected the Physitian may then try his skill
items.note: Paracelsus cited: cure by faith, or the physician after the purging.

items.quote: The Causes of those diseases that are of the Ens of God are unsearchable
items.note: Causes of these diseases are said to be beyond search.

items.quote: the predestinate Terme or period according to the Divine pleasure is to be observed
items.note: The set term recalls the Terme of Life of the first cause in CH5.68.

items.quote: A Physitian beginneth in appeasing Gods wrath.
items.note: Margin note: the physician begins by appeasing God.
